name: mirage
text:
Partly valid. The public-bias idea is real, but I wouldn't build a bid rule on it until the data backs it.

What supports it: our own study says prop Overs lose and totals win (2026-10-17), and BidTier already ranks prop Overs as risky. Bids on the Under side of props are the natural mirror of that.

What cuts against it:
1. Bids are priced off a sharp-book fair line (Pinnacle devigged). If the public inflates Overs and favorites, the sharp line has mostly already moved, so the public lean is partly priced into the fair line. Underdogs aren't a free edge. The favorite-longshot bias says longshots are overpriced, and that is the opposite of your underdog idea. Our rule of no buys under 20 cents exists for that reason.
2. Posting 'slightly under fair' is just a bid with a bigger margin. That raises the edge per fill but lowers the fill rate. And the fills you do get skew toward someone who knows more than you (adverse selection).
3. The bias is only a few percent, and it moves between sports and markets.

How I'd test it: split our settled bids and fills by side (Over/Under, favorite/underdog) and by kind. Judge by closing-line value first, then results, counting games rather than bets. If Unders and totals beat the close with the interval above zero, I'd lift their tier and size and add a small margin. If not, we skip it. Want me to run that split and report back?
